title: A personal financial statement: knowing what you actually have
subtitle: Net worth statement
openingQuestion: Mai wants to know exactly where her finances stand, but only looks at her bank account balance (150 million VND) and thinks that's her entire 'wealth', while she also has 300 million VND still owed on a car loan, a 200-million-VND savings book, and a 100-million-VND brokerage account. Which tool gives her the fullest, most accurate financial picture?
openingOptions: Checking the bank balance each day is enough to know where she stands
Adding up monthly income is enough, with no need to count her debts
No tool needed - her own sense of it is accurate enough to judge
Draw up a net worth statement: list every asset and subtract every debt
explanation: A personal net worth statement is a snapshot of your entire financial situation at a point in time, calculated as: Net worth = Total assets - Total debts. For Mai: total assets = 150 (cash) + 200 (savings) + 100 (stocks) = 450 million; total debt = 300 million (car loan); actual net worth = 450 - 300 = 150 million VND. Looking only at the bank balance risks misjudging the situation - the 150-million balance in the account doesn't reflect the 300-million debt hanging over it. A financial statement gives an honest, complete view, and is a mandatory starting point before drawing up any financial plan.

realWorldExample.company: Building a personal balance sheet in practice
realWorldExample.description: Many financial planners recommend updating a personal financial statement periodically (every quarter or every year), similar to how a business prepares a balance sheet. This helps catch warning signs early - for example, net worth not rising even as income rises steadily (usually because spending/debt rises to match it - the 'lifestyle inflation' effect covered in earlier lessons) - letting you adjust your spending and saving plan in time.

quiz.question: What is the formula for personal net worth?
options: Total income minus total expenses over a year
The total value of assets owned, with nothing subtracted
Total assets minus total debts (Assets - Liabilities)
The balances of every bank account added together
quiz.explanation: Net worth is the figure that most accurately reflects a person's true 'financial value', by taking everything they own and subtracting everything they owe.

quiz.question: Why is looking only at a bank account balance NOT enough to assess your personal financial situation?
options: Because the bank only updates the balance once a month
Because the balance is always lower than net worth by exactly the tax amount
Because the bank balance already includes real estate value
Because the balance doesn't reflect other debts and other assets
quiz.explanation: A complete financial picture needs to account for ALL assets and ALL debts, not just one single account - this is why a personal financial statement matters more than just checking one account's balance.

quiz.question: What does a personal net worth statement include?
options: All assets minus all debts, giving net worth
All income minus expenses for the year, giving the amount saved
A list of profitable investments only, excluding losing ones
A monthly income/expense report submitted to the tax authority at year-end
quiz.explanation: This is your own balance sheet: a snapshot at one point in time. Unlike an income/expense statement - which describes a period of time - it answers the question 'where do I stand'.

quiz.question: You live in a house with 1.5 billion still owed on a mortgage, market value 3 billion. How do you record it on the statement?
options: Just record the 3 billion under assets - the loan isn't part of this statement
Asset of 3 billion and debt of 1.5 billion, contributing 1.5 billion to net worth
Just record the 1.5 billion debt, since a home you live in isn't an investment
Record nothing at all, since the house hasn't been sold so it has no real value yet
quiz.explanation: Recording both sides is what shows the real picture. Someone who only records the home's value and forgets the loan will think they're exactly 1.5 billion richer than they actually are - the most common mistake in self-assessing finances.

quiz.question: How often should you redo a financial statement?
options: Only once in your life, at the point you start earning income
Once a week, to closely track the value changes of your investments
Once a year, or after every major event like changing jobs or buying a home
Only when a bank requires it during a loan application review
quiz.explanation: What's worth tracking isn't the absolute number but the trend across years: is net worth rising, and is it rising because of saving or because of the market. Once a year is enough to see that trend.

quiz.question: Why separate cash-flow-generating assets from consumption assets on the statement?
options: Because income-generating assets always rise in value while consumption assets always fall
Because the tax authority requires these two groups to be classified separately when declaring assets
Because consumption assets aren't counted toward personal net worth
Because only the first group can support you once you no longer have income from work
quiz.explanation: Someone with 5 billion in net worth but with all of it tied up in the home they live in and the car they drive has nothing to live on once they stop working. High net worth doesn't equal financial freedom.

keyTakeaways: Net worth = Total assets - Total debts - this is the single most important figure reflecting your true financial situation
List out every asset fully (cash, savings, securities, real estate) and every debt (home/car loans, credit cards) to calculate it correctly
Updating the financial statement periodically (quarterly/yearly) helps track the rising/falling trend in net worth over time, not just a single point
Net worth not rising despite rising income is a warning sign that your lifestyle is eating up or exceeding the extra income

practicePrompt.question: Khoa has 200 million in his bank account and thinks he's 'rich'. But he also owes 80 million on a credit card, 250 million on a car loan, while holding a 150-million savings book and 50 million in stocks. What is Khoa's actual net worth?
options: 70 million VND = total assets (200+150+50 = 400 million) minus total debt owed (80+250 = 330 million)
200 million VND, since just calculating the bank account balance alone is enough to accurately reflect the real financial situation
400 million VND, calculated as the sum of all assets without subtracting any current debt at all
330 million VND, calculated as the sum of all current debts without adding any asset at all
practicePrompt.explanation: Net worth = Total assets (400 million) - Total debt (330 million) = 70 million VND - a figure far lower than the feeling of being 'rich' from looking only at the 200-million bank balance.

summary.keyIdea: Net worth = Total assets - Total debts - this is the single most important figure reflecting your true financial situation
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: List out every asset fully (cash, savings, securities, real estate) and every debt (home/car loans, credit cards) to calculate it correctly

application.title: Calculate it now
application.message: Open your bank/brokerage app, add up the balances of every account and asset, subtract your total current debt - that's your real net worth today.
application.secondary: It doesn't need to be perfectly precise, just honest with yourself.

sections.text: Before drawing up any financial plan - buying a home, retiring early, investing long-term - the first question to answer honestly is: where do I actually stand right now? A personal financial statement is the tool that answers that question with a specific number.

A personal financial statement (net worth statement/balance sheet) is a list of all assets and debts at one point in time, similar to the balance sheet a business prepares each quarter. Unlike an income/spending statement (which reflects cash flow over a period), a financial statement is a 'snapshot' at the exact moment it's drawn up, showing your true financial value.
How to build a personal financial statement

The first step is listing all ASSETS: cash and checking accounts, savings books, brokerage/investment fund accounts, real estate (at estimated market value, not purchase price), a car/other valuable assets, life insurance with a surrender value (if any). The second step is listing all DEBTS: outstanding mortgage, car loan, credit card debt, consumer loans, loans from relatives (if any). Take total assets minus total debt, and the result is net worth.

items: Assets: cash, savings, securities/funds, real estate, other valuable assets
Debts: mortgage/car loans, credit card debt, consumer loans, loans from relatives
Net worth = Total assets - Total debts
Value real estate/assets at current MARKET value, not the original purchase price, for an accurate figure

sections.label: Why update it periodically, not just once
sections.text: The real value of a financial statement isn't the number at one point in time - it's the TREND over time. Updating it every quarter or every year lets you see whether net worth is rising, falling, or flat - and, more importantly, catch early if income is rising but net worth isn't rising to match (a sign your spending/lifestyle is 'eating up' the extra income).

lines: You can't plan a route to a destination if you don't know exactly where you're standing - a personal financial statement is that honest starting point.
Spending 30 minutes each quarter to update your financial statement is one of the simplest but most valuable habits in the whole journey of managing personal finances.
